faq.a: Take a focused developmental history, compare with age‑specific checklists, and perform a quick physical exam for red flags.
faq.q: What is the first step when a caregiver reports missed milestones?

faq.a: Perform a simple hearing screen; if abnormal, prioritize audiology; if normal, consider speech‑language therapy and other causes.
faq.q: How do you differentiate language delay from hearing loss?

faq.a: When there are focal neurological signs, regression, or suspicion of structural brain disease.

exam: A 10‑month‑old fails to sit unsupported – what are the three most likely reversible causes in a low‑resource setting? — Assess nutrition, anemia, and chronic infection (malaria/HIV).

During a routine check you note a child’s head circumference is <2 SD below mean – what does this suggest and what next step? — Possible microcephaly; obtain detailed prenatal history and screen for TORCH infections.

A caregiver reports loss of speech after a febrile illness – which red flag does this represent and what immediate investigation is warranted? — Regression; order malaria test, HIV rapid test, and consider neuroimaging if focal signs.
You suspect iron‑deficiency anemia contributing to delay – why avoid giving iron before ruling out infection? — Iron can exacerbate bacterial growth; confirm infection status first.
In a clinic without audiology equipment, how can you assess hearing in a 2‑year‑old? — Use behavioural observation (response to voice, startle to sound) and refer if abnormal.

A child with sickle cell disease shows motor delay – what specific complication should you look for? — Silent cerebral infarcts; consider MRI if available, otherwise monitor neuro‑development closely.
What community‑based intervention improves developmental outcomes in malnourished children? — Caregiver‑led play and responsive feeding programmes delivered by health workers.

How would you explain to parents the importance of early stimulation despite limited resources? — Simple daily activities (talking, singing, age‑appropriate toys) promote brain growth and are low‑cost.
ai.title: Developmental Milestones in Children
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: A framework for assessing growth across motor, language, social and cognitive domains, recognising red flags, and planning investigations and management in low‑resource settings.

b: Milestones are benchmarks, not strict cut‑offs; variation exists.
Use a structured history and age‑specific checklists (e.g., WHO child development standards).
sections.p: Developmental milestones are age‑appropriate abilities that reflect the maturation of the central nervous system. Clinicians assess four domains: gross/fine motor, language, social‑emotional, and cognition.

b: Mild: 1–3 months behind
Moderate: 3–6 months behind
Severe: >6 months behind or loss of previously acquired skills
sections.p: Delay is classified by the extent of lag behind expected age:

b: Prenatal: maternal infections (malaria, HIV, TORCH), malnutrition, toxin exposure.
Perinatal: birth asphyxia, prematurity, neonatal sepsis.
Post‑natal: chronic infections (TB, HIV), severe anemia, sickle cell disease, recurrent malaria, malnutrition, neglect, lack of stimulation.
sections.p: Identify whether the delay is global or domain‑specific and consider common tropical and low‑resource contributors.

b: Gross motor: inability to sit, crawl, or walk at expected ages.
Language: absent babbling, single words, or sentences.
Social: poor eye contact, lack of joint attention.
Cognition: failure to follow simple commands or solve puzzles.
sections.p: Parents report missed skills for the child’s age; clinicians observe reduced interaction, poor motor control, limited speech, or regression.

t.b: Assess nutritional status and possible chronic disease; low weight‑for‑age suggests malnutrition or systemic illness.

t.a: Basic labs (CBC, malaria rapid test, HIV rapid test, urine microscopy)
t.b: Detect anemia, malaria, HIV, urinary infection that can impair development; treat if positive.
Identify iron‑deficiency anemia, a reversible cause of delay; <11 g/dL in children <5 y indicates anemia.

t.a: If available, neuroimaging (cranial ultrasound or CT)
t.b: Evaluate structural brain lesions when focal deficits or regression are present; if unavailable, rely on clinical clues.

t.a: Hearing screen (otoacoustic emissions or simple click test)
t.b: Rule out hearing loss causing language delay; abnormal test warrants referral.
Use detailed clinical assessment, growth trends, and response to empiric treatment (e.g., deworming, iron supplementation).

b: Loss of previously acquired milestones.
Focal neurological signs (asymmetrical tone, seizures).
Severe malnutrition (MUAC <115 mm).
Persistent fever or chronic infection.
Infection: antimalarials, antiretroviral therapy, TB treatment per national protocol.
Anemia: oral iron (ferrous sulfate) after confirming iron deficiency; avoid in active infection without diagnosis.
Nutrition: therapeutic feeding (e.g., ready‑to‑use therapeutic food) for moderate‑severe acute malnutrition.
Stimulation: caregiver‑led play, responsive communication, community health worker home visits.
Referral: to physiotherapy, speech therapy, or specialist paediatric neurology when severe or progressive.
sections.p: Treat underlying causes, provide nutrition, and initiate early stimulation.

b: Re‑assess milestones every 3 months until age‑appropriate.
Vaccinate per EPI schedule; prevent malaria with nets and prophylaxis.
Promote exclusive breastfeeding, timely complementary feeding, and micronutrient supplementation (vitamin A, iron).
Educate caregivers on responsive interaction and safe play.
Global developmental delay vs. specific learning disorder (the latter occurs after normal early milestones).
Physical growth failure (stunting) which may coexist but is a separate measurement.
Normal hemoglobin does not exclude iron deficiency if ferritin is low; consider ferritin or transferrin saturation.
Negative malaria rapid test does not rule out low‑density parasitaemia; repeat if clinical suspicion persists.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe malnutrition (MUAC <115 mm) or failure to thrive
